speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: asked the Prime Minister given the new normal of endemic COVID-19 and shifts in global inflation dynamics (a) whether Singapore’s long-term inflation expectations are well anchored; (b) whether there is the risk of de-anchoring of inflation returning to our long-term target in a timely manner under current challenging global macroeconomic and supply conditions; and (c) whether there is also a risk that our current estimates of long-term inflation have risen.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The stabilisation of households’ longer-term inflation expectations occurred alongside a similar outturn in actual inflation in late 2022.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: On a month-on-month basis, the pace of increase in core prices has trended down over the second half of 2022.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: As the Member observed, multiple factors will influence the path of global, regional, and domestic inflation over the longer term.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: These include, for instance, demographics, technological advances that impact productivity, future trends in globalisation and central banks’ commitments to ensure low and stable inflation in their economies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: These factors can potentially boost or dampen inflation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: There is therefore uncertainty and a significant diversity of views among central bankers, academics and analysts on the likely inflation trends in the long term.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My first is in regard to the assessment of the long-term inflation by MAS and the Government.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How often would MAS or the Government assess the long-term inflation estimates, taking into consideration the changes in dynamics in commodity prices, global shifts and inflation dynamics?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The second question is related to what has happened overnight and things that have happened in the financial sector globally.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How does financial stability play a part in our exchange rate policy considerations and also long-term inflation?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If the Minister of State can also briefly share about the latest developments on financial stability, given overnight happenings, what impact do those have on inflation and Singapore's financial sector as well?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The longer-term inflation expectations are proxied by five-year ahead forecasts for inflation, both looking at professional forecasters as well as household expectations.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The household expectations survey, the DBS-SKBI SInDEx (Singapore Index of Inflation Expectations) Survey, as I mentioned, has shown that five-year ahead inflation forecasts have stabilised over the June and September surveys, and fell in the latest survey in December.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, it is a mixture of both professional forecasters as well as household expectations.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: With regard to the Member's second supplementary question, I will frame the context in terms of how that would be impacted by or affecting longer-term inflation.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: As Members know, MAS' monetary policy is medium-term focused to achieve low and stable inflation as the basis for Singapore's economic growth.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: MAS has tightened monetary policy since October 2021 and will continue to closely monitor global and domestic economic developments in the run-up to the scheduled policy review in April 2023, where it will take into account the implications for inflation as well as growth.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: By themselves, near-term shocks such as the recent developments in the international banking industry would not have direct implications for the long-term path of inflation and the Singapore Dollar Nominal Effective Exchange Rate (S$NEER).

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: As I mentioned in my earlier response, these depend on longer-term structural factors such as demographics, technology advances that impact productivity as well as future trends in globalisation.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But as the Member also observed, there have been developments overnight and earlier this morning, and I would like to point Members to the statement that MAS had issued this morning and other statements related to developments in the international banking sector on 16 March 2023 as well as 13 March 2023.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Allow me to make a few quick points.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Customers of Credit Suisse will continue to have full access to their accounts and Credit Suisse's contracts with counterparties remain in force.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Second, Singapore's banking system remains sound and resilient.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The Singapore dollar money market and foreign exchange market continue to function well.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Banks in Singapore are well-capitalised and conduct regular stress tests against credit and other risks.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Their liquidity positions are healthy, underpinned by a stable and diversified funding base.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: MAS will continue to closely monitor the domestic financial system and international developments and stands ready to provide the liquidity through its suite of facilities to ensure that Singapore's financial system remains stable and financial markets continue to function in an orderly manner.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Just a quick follow-up on the question about inflation expectations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I wonder if the Minister of State can elaborate on whether MAS has observed any evidence of inflation pressures actually passing through to wages, in particular?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And if so, what kind of mitigation mechanisms does the MAS have in terms of dealing with the possibility that this could become more entrenched?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: As MAS has also communicated, MAS Core Inflation is expected to ease more discernibly over the second half of 2023.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This reflects a combination of base effects and also moderating external and domestic labour cost pressures.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: It actually suggests that longer-term inflation expectations are unlikely to persistently increase.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Of course, we are looking at this and monitoring this very closely.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But more broadly, wages in Singapore are not tightly indexed to inflation.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Over the years, our tripartite wage-setting institutions have ensured that wage outcomes remain in line with productivity growth.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But we will closely monitor developments as they go.
